text: The bit-flip code's exact mirror image: same structure, same syndrome logic, but built in a rotated basis to catch the one error type the bit-flip code misses entirely.

Recall the X-basis states plus and minus. A phase-flip error does to plus and minus exactly what a bit-flip error does to zero and one — it swaps them. That's not a coincidence, it's the defining relationship between the X and Z bases, and it means you can build a phase-flip code by rotating the bit-flip code's entire construction. Encode logical zero as plus-plus-plus and logical one as minus-minus-minus, by first applying a Hadamard gate to the data qubit, then running the identical two-CNOT encoding circuit. A Z error on any one qubit now flips it between plus and minus, mirroring exactly how an X error flipped a qubit between zero and one.

Where the bit-flip code measured Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 to catch disagreements in the computational basis, this code measures X1X2 and X2X3 to catch disagreements in the Hadamard basis. Both stabilizers read plus-1 on the valid encoded states, and flip to minus-1 exactly when a Z error has hit one of the 3 qubits.

Representing plus as 0 and minus as 1, injecting a single Z error at each qubit position gives this verified table, starting from logical zero: no error gives syndrome 00. An error on qubit 1 gives syndrome 10, correct by applying Z to qubit 1. Qubit 2 gives syndrome 11, apply Z to qubit 2. Qubit 3 gives syndrome 01, apply Z to qubit 3. This is structurally the identical table to the bit-flip code's, with X error and flip-the-qubit replaced by Z error and apply-Z — exact because the X and Z bases play perfectly swapped roles under the Hadamard transform.

But exactly as the bit-flip code was blind to Z errors, this code is blind to X errors: an X error on one qubit leaves both X1X2 and X2X3 unchanged, since they commute with X errors, so the syndrome reads 00 even though the logical state has been corrupted. Neither 3-qubit code alone is a general-purpose code — each protects against exactly one error type.
The next lesson shows how combining both ideas, not just picking one, gives a code that handles an arbitrary single-qubit error: the Shor nine-qubit code.
